{"answer":"I chose the low-angle clip as the most informative extra source because it best exposes sequencing through the legs, trunk, arms, and seat travel: <vref id="019fb493-9535-7e00-905e-9e0e10563241" start="00:00" end="00:43"></vref>.

Direct observation: In repeated strokes visible around <vref id="019fb493-9535-7e00-905e-9e0e10563241" start="00:00" end="00:13"></vref> and again <vref id="019fb493-9535-7e00-905e-9e0e10563241" start="00:13" end="00:43"></vref>, the drive appears to begin with the legs, the torso starts swinging while the legs are still finishing, and the arm draw joins in late. The shins appear close to vertical at the catch, stroke length looks consistent, the handle path appears mostly level with a slight recovery dip to clear the knees, and there is a visible pause/settling at the finish before recovery.

Coaching interpretation: That visible overlap pattern — legs initiating, then trunk opening before leg extension is fully completed, with a brief finish pause — is a reasonable candidate mechanism to investigate for output differences at similar stroke rate, because small changes in sequencing sharpness or force concentration during the drive could affect watts without obviously changing cadence.

Does it prove the mechanism occurred in the selected workout windows? No. This angle provides a plausible visible pattern worth investigating, but it does not prove that this mechanism caused the approximately 58 W difference in the workout windows.
